Source: Synthetic Agricultural Load Data Generation Using TimeGANs
Abstract: In power system applications, accessing real data is one of the main challenges. Load modeling is an example that can be hampered by a lack of real data. This paper proposes synthetic data generation as a solution to deal with insufficient datasets. To this end, Timeseries Generative Adversarial Networks (TimeGANs) are proposed to create synthetic electricity data for an agricultural load. Center pivot irrigation system data is targeted, which does not exhibit the same trends as residential or commercial utility data, and information is presented in the lower dimensions. Obtained results show that TimeGANs can leverage the lower dimensional information to produce synthetic data with the same characteristics as the actual data. The proposed method can be utilized for modeling different electric loads.
Methods: Synthetic data generation using TimeGANs to create electricity load data for a center pivot irrigation agricultural load. The study uses an abstract-only experimental approach with no further formal methodology described.
Results: TimeGANs leveraged lower-dimensional information to produce synthetic data with the same characteristics as the actual agricultural load data.
Conclusions: Synthetic data generation can address insufficient load datasets, and the proposed method may be useful for modeling different electric loads.

Source: Using GEE to estimate soil moisture with data augmentation and SVR
Abstract: Soil moisture content is an important parameter in hydrological, meteorological, and agricultural applications. At present, soil moisture estimation with Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data shows great potential and promising practice. And some researches use machine learning methods to monitor soil moisture as more and more high-quality remote sensing data are available. However, the data driven feature of these methods brings a new challenge, i.e., every machine learning method needs sufficient in-situ data to be trained. Considering this problem, we proposed a data augmentation method based on alpha approximation method in this paper. Through this method, more training data can be produced, and then these data are provided to train a support vector regression (SVR) machine for soil moisture estimation. It turns out the SVR trained by original data and augmented data shows much better predictive capability than the SVR trained by original data only when using a proper data pretreatment and network, and it also obtains much better results than the original alpha approximation method. By contrast, the root mean squared error (RMSE) of our method decreased to 0.0339 and R2 increased to 0.6491. At last, Google Earth Engine (GEE) is used to collect relevant remote sensing data of Yancheng, Henan province and then soil moisture is estimated with our proposed method efficiently. In conclusion, a new method is proposed in this paper to meet the data driven feature of machine learning methods. And soil moisture of a region can be estimated efficiently by combining our method and the application of GEE.
Methods: Data augmentation based on the alpha approximation method was used to generate more training data, then a support vector regression (SVR) model was trained for soil moisture estimation. Google Earth Engine (GEE) collected remote sensing data for Yancheng, Henan province.
Results: The SVR trained on original plus augmented data performed better than SVR trained on original data only and better than the original alpha approximation method. RMSE decreased to 0.0339 and R2 increased to 0.6491.
Conclusions: A new data augmentation method can address limited in-situ training data for machine learning soil moisture estimation. Combining the method with GEE enables efficient regional soil moisture estimation.

Source: ICIP 2025 COMPETITION ON BEYOND VISIBLE SPECTRUM: AI FOR AGRICULTURE
Abstract: The ICIP 2025 “Beyond Visible Spectrum: AI for Agriculture” competition advanced the integration of hyperspectral imaging (HSI) and AI to support precision farming. It featured two key tasks: (1) automated crop disease diagnosis using real UAV-based HSI data, and (2) synthetic HSI generation via advanced generative models. These tasks tackled two major challenges: extracting informative features from high-dimensional spectral data and overcoming the scarcity of annotated datasets for training reliable AI systems. The competition convened global researchers, industry experts, and students to develop innovative, practical solutions for modern agriculture. Participants employed diverse AI approaches, ranging from efficient machine learning methods like XGBoost to deep learning architectures such as lightweight 3D CNNs, Vision Transformers (ViTs), GANs, and conditional diffusion models.Notably, winning solutions showed that well-designed traditional models can outperform deep networks in certain contexts. Generative models proved especially promising for augmenting spectral data and simulating crop diseases, improving model robustness. The challenge drew 181 teams from over 10 countries, resulting in 1,450+ submissions underscoring global interest in scalable, AI-enabled agricultural solutions. Outcomes demonstrated advances in spectral-spatial modelling, enabling earlier, more accurate disease detection and synthetic dataset creation to enhance the generalisability of AI systems in real-world farming.
Methods: Competition with two tasks: UAV-based hyperspectral crop disease diagnosis and synthetic HSI generation using generative models. Participants used XGBoost, lightweight 3D CNNs, ViTs, GANs, and conditional diffusion models.
Results: 181 teams from over 10 countries produced 1,450+ submissions. Winning solutions showed well-designed traditional models could outperform deep networks in some contexts, and generative models improved robustness via spectral data augmentation.
Conclusions: The competition advanced spectral-spatial modelling for earlier, more accurate disease detection and synthetic dataset creation in precision agriculture. A key limitation was the scarcity of annotated hyperspectral datasets.

Source: ASDGM: Agriculture Framework for Crops Data Generation and Recommendation
Abstract: Providing an accurate crop recommendation system becomes a significant challenge due to the limited, inconsistent, and privacy concerns of agricultural datasets. Especially when addressing global food security issues. Therefore, the work in this paper aims to generate Agriculture Synthetic Data based on Generative Models (ASDGM) as an applicable solution to enhance data accessibility while protecting sensitive information. In ASDGM multiple generative models have been applied, including GAN-based architectures (e.g., WCGAN-GP, CTGAN, and CTAB-GAN+), Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic model for tabular data (e.g., TabDDPM), and Tabular Variational AutoEncoder (TVAE). The synthetic datasets generated by generative models were evaluated using multiple metrics that measure distributional similarity, structural fidelity, predictive performance, and privacy preservation. Experimental results demonstrate that models such as TabDDPM provide robust performance across all metrics, maintaining data utility and privacy. The objectives of the ASDGM framework were twofold. First, ASDGM extended a benchmark crop recommendation dataset of 2,200 records to a modified synthetic dataset of 220,000 records using the TabDDPM generative model. Second, the modified dataset was used to train five machine learning classifiers, resulting in improved accuracy and F1-scores compared to training on the original dataset. The results support the integration of synthetic data generation with agricultural machine learning systems, enabling accurate crop recommendations under data-scarce and privacy-constrained conditions.
Methods: ASDGM used multiple generative models for agricultural synthetic data generation, including WCGAN-GP, CTGAN, CTAB-GAN+, TabDDPM, and TVAE. The synthetic data were evaluated with metrics for distributional similarity, structural fidelity, predictive performance, and privacy preservation.
Results: TabDDPM showed robust performance across all evaluation metrics while maintaining data utility and privacy. It expanded a 2,200-record crop recommendation dataset to 220,000 synthetic records and improved accuracy and F1-scores for five classifiers.
Conclusions: Synthetic data generation can support accurate crop recommendation under data-scarce and privacy-constrained conditions. The approach integrates generative models with agricultural machine learning systems.

Source: Precision Agriculture: Improving Water Stress Forecasting in Tomato Plants Using Bioristor Data and Advanced ML Techniques
Abstract: The water stress in crops, especially tomato plants, is highly challenging to yields and qualities. This study involves improving the forecasting of water stress by using Bioristor sensor information combined with advanced machine learning models. Bioristor sensors capture ion concentration changes in plant saps; hence very crucial real-time data. We developed models such as RNN, LSTM, Bi-GRU, and ARIMA, for predictions and time series forecasting. We applied the models on classification with Decision Trees as well as Random Forest. The performance of the model was measured using applications in accuracy, precision, recall, and confusion matrix analysis metrics, when predicting 1 and 24 hours in advance, using classifications of 2-state (stressed vs. not stressed) and 4-state (healthy, stressed, uncertain, recovery). Our results suggest promising accuracy for the prediction of water-stress conditions, offering a framework which may be applied in real-world precision agriculture to optimize strategies for water management.
Methods: Forecasting water stress in tomato plants using Bioristor sensor data with RNN, LSTM, Bi-GRU, ARIMA, Decision Trees, and Random Forest. Performance was evaluated for 1- and 24-hour-ahead prediction in 2-state and 4-state classifications using accuracy, precision, recall, and confusion matrix metrics.
Results: The models showed promising accuracy for predicting water-stress conditions. Results were reported for 1- and 24-hour-ahead forecasts across 2-state and 4-state classifications, but no exact metrics are provided in the abstract.
Conclusions: Bioristor data combined with machine learning may support real-world precision agriculture and water-management optimization. The abstract does not report limitations.

Source: Crop yield prediction via explainable AI and interpretable machine learning: Dangers of black box models for evaluating climate change impacts on crop yield
Abstract: Statistical crop modeling is pivotal for understanding climate impacts on crop yields. Choices of models matter: Linear regression is interpretable but limited in predictive power; machine learning predicts well but often remains a black box. To develop explainable artificial intelligence (AI) for exploring historical crop yield data and predicting crop yield, here we reported a Bayesian ensemble model (BM) that is interpretable with great explanatory and predictive power. BM embraces many competitive models via Bayesian model averaging, fits complex functions, and quantifies model uncertainty. Long-term crop yields are driven by both climate and technology; the common practice of first detrending and then analyzing the detrended data has an incorrigible bias. Therefore, BM was also aimed at decomposing historical yield data to jointly estimate technological trends and climate effects on crop yield. We compared BM with ElasticNet, Neural Network, MARS, SVM, Random Forests, and XGBoost. BM excelled at both predicting and explaining. When tested on synthetic data, BM was the only method unveiling the true relationships: BM has stronger interpretability; other methods predicted well but for wrong reasons. When tested on maize yield data in Ohio, BM detected two technological shifts, attributable to hybrid corn adoption in the 1940′s and the technological slowing-down in the 1970′s: No other methods detected such changepoints. BM derived nonlinear asymmetric crop responses to climate and non-negligible temperature-precipitation interacting effects, with patterns consistent with theoretical or experimental evidence. Extrapolation of all the models for future yield prediction was highly uncertain, but BM provided more reliable predictions under novel climate whereas Random Forests and XGBoost proved unsuitable for extrapolation. Overall, BM provided new insights unattainable by the existing black-box methods. We caution against blind use of black-box machine learning for statistical crop modeling and call for more efforts to apply interpretable machine learning for mechanistic understandings of crop-climate interactions.
Methods: Bayesian ensemble regression model (BM) using Bayesian model averaging and MCMC was developed and compared with 10 alternatives across four experiments. Three synthetic datasets and 103 years of Ohio maize yield data (88 counties) were used, with predictive accuracy and explanatory power assessed via RMSE, PDPs, variable importance, and changepoint diagnostics.
Results: BM had the lowest error in the first experiment (RMSE 0.5; next best 2.99 for NN) and was the only method to recover the true model structure. In Ohio data, BM detected two technological shifts and nonlinear, asymmetric temperature-precipitation interactions; RF and XGBoost were poor for extrapolation.
Conclusions: Interpretable Bayesian machine learning outperformed black-box models for both prediction and explanation, and was more reliable for extrapolating to novel climate. The main caveat is that historical data limit identifiability and extrapolation remains uncertain, especially far outside the observed climate range.
